posts.cooked:
I am always frustrated when dnf5 pulls some doubtful stuff to my system with no indication why.

For example, dnf install -y gcc graphviz libffi-devel python3-devel python3-psycopg2 pulls in openh264 video codec, which is really undesirable on a headless box used for compiling stuff. There is also a lot of stuff I am almost 100% sure I don’t need.

It may be graphviz or any of its dependencies. I am certain that with some dnf and rpm commands I could find out the ancestor branch of openh264, but… there are two problems..

  1. I could never remember the rpm/dnf syntax, so I keep opening Google search to get one.
  2. Typing commands in terminal may work for a single package, but if I want to do a quick check “why a certain package is being pulled in” on each update, that is not practical.

So, what I want is the Web UI (because I still have to open the browser) where I paste a package list like gcc graphviz libffi-devel python3-devel python3-psycopg2 and it renders the dependencies tree top down down with these packages listed at the top and connections going down. And when I click the dependency, it should highlight the path to the top.

Maybe such tool exists already. Please paste your link if you’ve found one. Maybe it could be added to https://packages.fedoraproject.org

posts.name: Gregory Lee Bartholomew
posts.cooked:
A simple way to do that from the command line is to run, e.g., dnf install gcc graphviz libffi-devel python3-devel python3-psycopg2. As long as you omit the -y, dnf will display a list of what will be downloaded before it downloads the packages and prompt for confirmation. I don’t know why online examples everywhere show that command with the -y. They shouldn’t.

I don’t know if there is a way to get dnf to show the output of what is about to be installed as a dependency tree. If it doesn’t have that feature already, IMO it would be a reasonable feature request for the dnf package.

posts.cooked:
Gregory Lee Bartholomew:

A simple way to do that from the command line

Maybe I was not clear enough. I want to inspect the dependency chain through which openh264 package is pulled. The output from dnf install is present in the first post (maybe it is not evident, because it is wrapped by docker-compose timestamps and debug info). And the output doesn’t show the exact path to pulling openh264 - it only shows starting nodes and ending leaves with no connections between them.

posts.name: Gregory Lee Bartholomew
posts.cooked: Well, I’m not sure that it would get much use. Having dnf install show the dependency tree directly seems more useful to me, but if you want to open a RFE against that packages web app, I think the repo for it is here: https://forge.fedoraproject.org/apps/fedora-packages-static
